newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French public pay offer raises strike fears.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French public pay offer raises strike fears.

text.p: The French government offered public employees on Tuesday a 2.8 percent pay rise over two years, angering union leaders and raising fears of fresh strikes in the civil service sector.

The Communist-led CGT trade union broke the news of the 1997-98 offer after meeting Civil Service Minister Dominique Perben, saying the proposals ignored a key demand from unions for a big enough hike to make up for a pay freeze in 1996.

"What is important in the face of this kind of attitude is that employees make themselves heard loud and clear," the CGT said in a statement, adding that unions would meet in the evening to consider their response.
A Civil Service ministry official declined to comment but said Perben would hold a news conference at the end of the day (1700 GMT).

The 1996 civil service pay freeze was one of several union gripes behind crippling public sector strikes in late 1995 and the CGT said Perben had made it clear there was "no question" of making up for the 1996 freeze in the latest pay round.

Unions had warned in advance that they would fight any offer which failed to make at least "a gesture" to compensate for the loss of purchasing power last year, and that their response could include a strike in March.

The latest stand-off took place just hours before a rail strike called by the CGT and a protest rally by the Socialist CFDT union against government reforms which they say amount to a "break-up" of the SNCF railway network, threatening jobs and the rail monopoly.

The strike, set to begin at midnight and continue until 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) on Thursday, could reduce services by up to a half on some main and regional lines though Eurostar high-speed trains between Paris and London and fast train links between Paris and Brussels should be unaffected, SNCF said.

Unions staged a 36-hour stoppage last Thursday, warning that the proposal to break up the rail network, being debated in the National Assembly on Tuesday, would augur badly for jobs and working conditions.

On the pay issue, Perben was meeting unions one by one to present a government offer covering some six million workers in central administration, local government, education, health and transport jobs.
"Is this the kind of framework in which the minister asks about the possibility of opening 'negotiations'?" asked the militant CGT. "Negotiate what? A fall in purchasing power?"

Pierre Avignon, head of the moderate white-collar CGC union, said last week that unions wanted negotiations but would consider a strike if they got a unilateral offer which fell short of their demands.

Jean-Pierre Gualezzi, head of the Unsa union grouping, said in an interview in the newspaper Les Echos on Tuesday that the union meeting later in the day was likely to result in a one-day strike call.
Civil servants staged a one-day strike last October 17 over pay and government plans to cut their number by nearly 6,000 this year under the 1997 budget.

About a third of civil servants stayed away from work that day, according to the civil service ministry, and unions held off on follow-up action after Prime Minister Alain Juppe signalled that pay talks could be reopened.
